p: The first week of August, Aurora ran out of shade. Jordan worked a Monday shift that started at seven in the morning with a roofer who'd stopped sweating, and her last call ended at three the next morning with a man in his eighties who'd fallen asleep in his garage with the door down and a box fan blowing hot air at him. Somewhere in the middle her partner said the truck's thermometer read 101, and neither of them laughed, because they'd already been to two of those calls and were about to go to a third.

Heat is a protocol. You cool them, you watch the pressure, you don't let them stand up too fast. She'd done it a hundred times. What she'd never done was think about what the same afternoon did to a 1978 Cessna sitting on the ramp at Centennial with its wings in the sun.
Tuesday night, slept out and showered, she was eating cold noodles on the couch when Claire called. Claire didn't call. Claire texted, in full sentences, with periods.

Ellie wants to go up in the airplane, Claire said, without saying hello. She's been asking since she was six. Danny always said when she's tall enough. She measured herself on the pantry door last night. She marked it with a Sharpie. A pause. Jordan could hear the dishwasher running on the other end. If Abby flies it. If you're in it. And if she goes, I go. That's the deal.
Jordan put the noodles down. Okay.
Saturday the fifteenth. I'm on days all week. Three o'clock is the only time I've got. Another pause. Don't make it a thing. I'll change my mind.
After she hung up Jordan sat there for a while. Then she texted Abby, and the answer came back before she'd set the phone down.

A text from Abby Strand. I can do the 15th at 3. Four of us, August, 3 in the afternoon. You're going to do the numbers. All of them. Thursday 8am, briefing room. Bring Biscuit's POH from the seat back and a pencil.

Wednesday she drove to the airport after her nap and got the POH out of the seat back pocket. Biscuit was tied down in her spot on the ramp with the sunshade in the windshield and the yoke lock in, and the cabin was hotter than the back of the ambulance. The book was soft at the corners, held together with clear packing tape along the spine. Section 5 was the most worn. On the takeoff distance page somebody had drawn a pencil box around the 8,000 foot row in the 2,300 pound block, and written next to it in small block capitals: THIS IS AUGUST.
She knew whose capitals those were.
At 8:10 Abby wrote the morning's two lines on the whiteboard. The air conditioner in the briefing room window was running full blast and doing about as much good as a dog panting at the sun.
KAPA, Thursday 6:53 AM, and the forecast for 1 PM. METAR KAPA 061253Z 18004KT 10SM SKC 17/07 A3006 RMK AO2. Forecast for 1900Z: wind 330 at 10, temperature 34°C, altimeter 29.90
We're going to fly at one this afternoon, on purpose, in the heat, so you know what you're asking Biscuit for next Saturday. Pressure altitude at one o'clock. Show me how you got it.
Jordan had the POH open in front of her, the pencil box on the 8,000 foot row staring up at her.

Yep. Low pressure, the airplane thinks it's higher than it is. She writes 5,905 in the corner of the board and draws a box around it. Everything this afternoon starts from that box. Don't make me erase it.
Next. Density altitude, one o'clock, and then tell me what it means for us in real words. Not test words.

Jordan worked it on the legal pad. Standard temperature at 5,905 feet. Then the difference. Then times 120. She checked it twice, the way she checked a drip rate, and then a third time because Abby was watching.

Yep. She writes it under the box. 9,600. Then she writes 5,885 next to it and draws a long arrow between them. That's almost four thousand feet of mountain we didn't have to climb to get there. The engine and the prop think they're up there, and so does the wing. The runway's the only thing still at 5,885.

Tucked into the back of the POH, behind Section 6, was an index card in a plastic sleeve. Danny's capitals again. BISCUIT W&B. EMPTY 1,438 39.1. ME 185. FULL FUEL 240. Under that, a column of loading combinations he'd worked out and a smiley face next to the bottom one.
Jordan held it up. Abby didn't take it. Before you use anything on that card, go ask Marisol where she keeps the airplane's records. Then decide which empty weight you believe.
Marisol was at her bench in the hangar with a carburetor in pieces on a shop towel. She looked at the card, and something went across her face and came back.

Marisol pulls a binder off the shelf over the bench and opens it to a tab marked W&B. On top is a form with her own signature on it, dated October 2019. ADS-B box, the panel GPS, the antenna, the wiring. I weighed her on scales after. 1,486 at 39.5. She looks at the card in Jordan's hand. That card's from before. He never redid it. I told him to. She closes the binder and hands it over. Forty eight pounds, she's gained. Same as Walt since 1978.

Back in the briefing room, with the binder, Abby slid the blank worksheet across the table. This afternoon. You, me, full tanks, our two flight bags and a gallon of water in the back, because it's August and I'm not dying of heatstroke over Bennett. Weight and balance. Go.
I'm one fifty with boots on. I'll say it once.
Jordan had a pencil in her hand and the urge, which she noticed and didn't like, to say two people is obviously fine.

She does it in pencil, in neat columns, the way she'd chart vitals. 2,058 pounds. 83,661 pound inches. 40.65. She checks the forward limit at that weight and gets 36.08. Inside, with room. Abby reads it upside down and doesn't say anything, which is how Jordan knows it's right. Then she says, Now keep that sheet. Saturday you'll add two people to it.
Now the takeoff table. 2,058 pounds, 5,905 feet, 34 degrees. Tell me which numbers you're going to use and why.

Biscuit's POH, Section 5. Short field takeoff distance. FLAPS 10°. FULL THROTTLE PRIOR TO BRAKE RELEASE. PAVED, LEVEL, DRY RUNWAY. ZERO WIND.. GROUND ROLL TOTAL TO CLEAR 50 FT OBSTACLE, FEET. 2300 LB   20°C         30°C         40°C 5000      1175/2120  1265/2290  1360/2475 6000      1290/2350  1390/2550  1495/2760 7000      1420/2620  1530/2850  1645/3090 8000      1565/2935  1690/3200  1815/3480 2100 LB   20°C         30°C         40°C 5000       955/1750  1030/1890  1105/2040 6000      1050/1935  1130/2095  1215/2270 7000      1155/2155  1245/2340  1340/2535 8000      1275/2410  1375/2620  1480/2845 NOTES: 1. Prior to takeoff from fields above 3000 ft elevation, lean the mixture for maximum RPM in a full throttle, static runup.. 2. Decrease distances 10% for each 9 knots headwind. For operation with tailwinds up to 10 knots, increase distances by 10% for each 2 knots.. 3. For operation on a dry, grass runway, increase distances by 15% of the "ground roll" figure.
In pencil, off to the side of the 8,000 foot row in the 2,300 pound block, was the box and the word AUGUST.

Why 2,100 and not 2,058? It's the next heavier block. Round toward worse. And why interpolate the temperature? Because thirty four is a real number and I have it. Abby nods once and gets up to refill her coffee from the machine, which has been making the same burnt smell since Jordan's first lesson in April, and says over her shoulder, Weight and altitude, round up. Temperature you can work. Now do the wind, and don't look at me while you do it, I'm not going to make a face. She makes a face anyway when Jordan writes cosine, but it's the good one.

At 12:50 the ramp was shimmering like a parking lot in a car commercial. The tie down ropes were hot enough that Jordan untied them with her sleeves pulled down over her hands, and when she got in, the yoke was too hot to hold, so she sat there with the door open and the little air vents blowing on it until she could. Somebody two rows over was washing a Bonanza and the water was drying on the wing before he could get the chamois to it. The ATIS said wind three two zero at one zero, temperature three four, altimeter two niner niner zero, runway three five right, and a temperature she'd already turned into a density altitude on the legal pad in her lap.

The run up went fine. She leaned for max RPM at full throttle like the note said, and watched the tach climb as she did it, which was a strange thing to watch, a number getting better because she'd taken something away. At the hold short line, Abby said:
Before you go. Where do you quit?

Good. Say it out loud on the roll. So she does. Throttle in, brakes off. Biscuit gets going like a grocery cart with one bad wheel. Airspeed alive. Forty. Taxiway coming. Off before it by a few hundred feet. Jordan had wanted more.

The second takeoff Abby wanted from 35L, the shorter one, seven thousand feet, so Jordan could see a runway end that wasn't a rumor. She'd pulled back a little early. She knew it right away, the way she knew a bad stick in a patient's arm before the flash didn't come. Biscuit came off the runway and then just hung there about five feet up. The stall horn beeped once and stopped. The airspeed was two knots under the grease pencil mark Abby had put on the glass that morning, which Marisol was going to complain about cleaning off. There was still plenty of runway out ahead. After that there was the airport fence, and a road, and then the long beige roofs of a business park with heat coming off them.
Abby's hands were in her lap. They stayed there.

Jordan puts the nose down about two degrees. She hates doing it, and some animal part of her keeps hating it for the whole two seconds it takes, which on the clock in her head is about a week. The horn stops. The airspeed comes up to the mark. Then she lets the nose come up and Biscuit climbs out over the fence and the road and the business park, slowly, while some guy in a parking lot down there stops loading his truck to watch. Abby lets out a breath. Ground effect. It's only about a wingspan tall, so thirty six feet on her. Then it's gone. You did fine. She writes GE on her kneeboard and underlines it, and they don't talk again until the reservoir.

They climbed east to 7,500 under the shelf. It took a while. Abby had her time it, and it was about 520 feet a minute with just the two of them, which Jordan wrote on her kneeboard under the 5,905 and the 9,600, because she had a feeling she was going to want all three of those numbers again on Saturday. Out past the reservoir the plains were brown already, a month early, and the wheat that was left had been cut into stubble that threw heat up at them in bumps you could see coming only because the dust devils marked them. Over Bennett it was bumpy enough that her pencil left the kneeboard twice. A water bottle rolled around on the floor the whole lesson. Jordan was pretty sure it was hers.
On the way in, Abby said, Feel how much back pressure she wants? It's just us up front and a water jug in back. Saturday you'll have Claire and Ellie back there. What's different?

Yep. And a knot faster in cruise, which nobody at the club has ever noticed, including Russ, who'd notice a free knot from across the street. She taps the trim wheel between the seats with her boot. We're nose heavy today, so you've been rolling in nose up the whole way down final like you're winding a clock. Saturday you'll need less. Trim it like today and she'll balloon on you right over the numbers with Claire watching.

Sunday it was 97 in Parker and Claire's air conditioner was making a noise like a dentist's drill in the next room. The three of them ended up on the kitchen floor in front of the open freezer, eating grape popsicles, because Ellie said that was the rule over 95 and nobody could prove otherwise.
Ellie knew about Thursday. Ellie knew about all of it. Claire knew about all of it, from Abby, by text. Jordan filed that away to be weird about later.
Mom says Biscuit had a hard time getting up because it was hot. She licked the side of her popsicle where it was running. Does the airplane get tired?

Claire looked at Jordan over the top of Ellie's head, with her own popsicle melting down her wrist. It was the same look as in June, on the trampoline, when Ellie wanted to know about clouds, and it meant the same thing: you're up.

Ellie thinks about it. Like when you run at the top of a mountain. Exactly like that. Same lungs, less air in every breath. Her engine has to breathe it, and her propeller has to push on it, and her wings have to sit on it, and when it's hot there's just less of it to go around. So she's not tired. She's out of breath. That's better than how I said it. Ellie, very satisfied, finishes the popsicle and then, with the stick still in her mouth: Is she going to be out of breath on Saturday? Claire gets up to shut the freezer and stands there with her back to them a little too long.
Wednesday evening Walt was in the hangar when she came by, sitting on Marisol's stool with his glasses on the end of his nose and a sheet of paper on his knee. He didn't say hello. He held it out.
Russ is taking two guys from his softball team to Greeley Sunday morning for golf. He did his own numbers. He says they work. Check them.

Russ's loading sheet, Sunday. EMPTY        1486 39.5   58,697 RUSS FRONT)   180 37     6,660 MIKE BACK)    190 73   13,870 DEV BACK)     190 73   13,870 CLUBS        120 95   11,400 FUEL 20 GAL    120 48    5,760 TOTAL       2286          110,257 CG 48ish. UNDER GROSS. GOOD TO GO. (the guys like the back, more legroom)
Jordan did the division on her phone. 48.23. She opened the POH to the envelope. Aft limit 47.3, at every weight.

She shows Walt the work. 190 pounds times 36 inches, divided by 2,286. 2.99. New CG 45.24. Inside, with room. Walt reads it twice. Send it to him. Not me. You. She does. Russ answers in four minutes: wait the back is NOT more legroom?? Then: ok dev sits up front. he's going to want the window. this is a nightmare. thank you. Walt stands up and puts the stool back where Marisol keeps it, exactly, and on his way out he says, That's twice now. She doesn't know what the first time was.

Thursday the 13th was hotter than the week before. Abby wanted one more hot takeoff before Saturday, then pattern work, then out. At the hold short Jordan did the run up and the mag check, and the radio got busy, and the tower cleared them for takeoff with a Citation on a three mile final.

Full throttle. Brakes off. Something was off. The tach was lower than last week. Not a lot. Maybe a hundred RPM, and with the tach reading fifty high to begin with, she didn't trust her own math. The airplane was rolling, just slowly. Her abort point, a taxiway she'd picked off the diagram, was coming up, and the airspeed needle was a long way from where it had been at that taxiway last Thursday.
Her eyes went to the red knob. All the way in. Full rich. She'd pushed it in for the mag check and never pulled it back.

Idle. Brakes. Nose dips. Centerline, mostly. She gets it off at the next taxiway with her pulse up where it lives on a three story carry down. Centennial Tower, Cessna Niner One Echo, rejected takeoff, clear of the runway. Tower says roger like she's asked for the time. On the taxiway she leans it out, full throttle, brakes on, and the tach comes up a hundred and twenty. She points at it. Abby nods. There you go. Screwed up, found out, still on the ground. That's the good version. Second try, they're off well before the taxiway.

Saturday, 2:30, Claire's Subaru pulled up by the hangar. Ellie was out before it stopped. Shorts, soccer cleats (lucky, she said, they'd won twice in them), and Danny's old Hangar Six cap, on the last hole and still down over her eyebrows. Booster cushion under one arm. Claire had left the soft cooler of waters in the Subaru, and she had the face of somebody who'd talked herself into this for the whole length of Jordan Road.
At three the ATIS said thirty five degrees, altimeter two niner eight two, wind variable at four. Jordan had the worksheet from Thursday on a clipboard. Two lines were blank.
Your worksheet, Abby said. How are you getting their numbers?
Against the hangar wall sat Marisol's big flat scale on casters. Parts, luggage, and one time, for reasons nobody would explain to Jordan, a goat.

Ellie thinks the airplane scale is the best thing that's happened all summer. 76 in cleats and the cap. Booster, 3. Claire gets on, gets off, says nothing. Abby, 150, as advertised. Jordan, 162 in boots. Bags and water, 20. Pencil, blank lines, done. From the bench Marisol says, mostly to the carburetor, First time anybody's used that thing for the airplane.

She did the worksheet on the hood of Claire's Subaru. The briefing room was a hundred yards off and losing its own fight with the heat. Everybody stood there and watched her, and she hated it. Pencil. One line, then the next. No talking. Like charting a code after.

Biscuit weight and balance, Saturday August 15, 3 PM. ITEM WEIGHT ARM MOMENT. Basic empty (Marisol, Oct 2019): 1,486 39.5 58,697. Front seats, Jordan 162, Abby 150: 312 37.0 11,544. Rear seats, Claire 174, Ellie 76, booster 3: 253 73.0 18,469. Fuel, 40 gal usable (Russ topped off at noon): 240 48.0 11,520. Baggage, 2 flight bags, 1 gal water: 20 95.0 1,900. TOTAL: 2,311 CG 44.19 102,130. MAX 2,300. OVER BY 11.. Without baggage or water: 2,291 CG 43.75 100,230. Under by 9.. PA 5,985. Standard 3.0°C. OAT 35°C. DA about 9,820.. Takeoff, 2,300 block, 6,000 row, 35°C, no wind: 1,443 ground roll, 2,655 over 50 ft.. Climb, 2,300 lb, 6,000 ft, 35°C: about 410 fpm.
She read it twice. Went back to the top and added it again. Same number. Of course.
Talk me through it, Abby said. She wasn't going to make the call. She'd said so Tuesday night, more or less, and she meant it.

We're eleven over. If we leave every bag and the water on the ramp, we're nine under. Nine pounds. On the hottest day this summer, at almost ten thousand feet of density altitude, which is the worst Biscuit can do. Four hundred feet a minute up, through the bumps, at seventy five hundred, which is sixteen hundred feet over Parker with the cumulus going up. She heard herself and kept going. The runway's fine. The runway isn't the problem. It's legal by nine pounds and a jug of water, and I'd be doing it because it's legal.
Nobody said anything. Out on the ramp the heat came up off the concrete in sheets and made the hangars across the way wobble. Somewhere a Cirrus was doing its run up and it sounded tired too.

I'd fly it, Abby said, finally. Legally. I've flown worse. And I'd spend the whole climb with my hand next to the throttle, wishing I'd said no in the parking lot. She looked at Jordan. Your numbers. Your call.

Jordan wrote one more line at the bottom of the sheet. SEPT, 7 AM, 14°C, A3010, 20 GAL: 2,191 LB WITH BAGS, CG 43.98, DA ABOUT 6,950. She'd worked it out last night, in case, and hadn't told anybody, because doing the math for the no felt like deciding it.
Then she crouched down in front of Ellie, on the hot concrete, so they were eye to eye under the brim of the cap.
Ellie looked at her, then at the airplane, then at her mother, then back. She'd measured herself on the pantry door. She'd worn her lucky cleats. But it's legal. You said.

It's legal. Barely. You know how Biscuit gets out of breath when it's hot? Today she'd be out of breath with all four of us and the gas, the whole way up. I don't want your first time to be her worst day. I want it to be her best one.
Your dad promised when you were tall enough. You're tall enough. It's the airplane that isn't ready today.

It didn't help. Ellie's chin went first. Jordan had seen that on a lot of kids in the back of the rig. Then Ellie was crying, hard, and Danny's cap fell off on the concrete, and she stepped on it with a cleat and didn't notice. Claire picked her up. Ellie was too big to carry and Claire carried her anyway, and looked at Jordan over Ellie's head.

Jordan expected anger. She'd have understood it. What she got was a nod. Small. The same one Claire gave doctors in the ER, Jordan figured, when they said the thing nobody wanted to hear and said it right.
Later Jordan would think about how easy it would have been to guess. Four people in a 172, a kid, a lap around the airport. Every guess she could have made would have come out under.

Claire carried Ellie to the car and sat in the back seat with her with the door open and the engine running for the air. Abby went inside without saying anything, which was the kindest thing anyone did all afternoon. Marisol put the scale back against the wall and put the booster cushion on top of it, carefully, like it was going to be needed.

Jordan walked out to Biscuit. She took the sunshade down and opened the door and sat in the left seat with the door open, the vinyl hot enough through her jeans to make her jump. By the mag switch, Ellie's sticker: HI DAD, in purple marker, the corners curling up in the heat. She took the green notebook out of her bag. She'd been reading it in order, mostly. She didn't do that today. She went looking for August, and found July, close enough.

Danny's logbook, a page from July, ten years ago. July 23. KAPA local, rental 172 from the school, 0.6. 94 degrees. Me, Claire, Tomás and Bree from Claire's work in back, full tanks, cooler in the baggage, because we were going to fly over Cherry Creek at sunset and it was going to be great. Walt was at the fuel truck and asked what we weighed. I said "not much." Ha. Asked for 28 because it was right there. Used most of it. MOST OF IT. 4,800 feet and the wheels came off somewhere past where I could see the end, and then she just hung there over the fence and thought about it. Climbed like a shopping cart. Took forever to get to pattern altitude. Claire held my knee the whole time and didn't say anything, which was worse than yelling. Back on the ground I did the math I should have done before. Over gross. Didn't lean either. New rule: W&B on paper every time there's more than two of us. If it's hot, do it twice. Claire says don't write down that she was there because she's not sure she was supposed to be flying. I said I don't write anything down. (+1 aboard. She doesn't know I know. Due in March.)
Jordan read it twice, and then a third time on the last line, and then she sat with her hand flat on the page for a long time.

Ten years ago in July. Due in March. Ellie had been in the back of an overloaded 172 on a 94 degree day, hanging over the fence on runway 28, before she was anybody. Before Danny was anybody's dad. He'd known. He'd written it in parentheses.

The right door opened. Claire, folding herself in like the seat might bite. She pulled the door to but didn't latch it. Red eyes, dry now. Out cold. Cried herself to sleep in the back seat. Marisol's in the car with her, doing a crossword out loud. She looked at the notebook. Which one's that?
Jordan handed it over, open. Claire read. Jordan could tell exactly when she hit the parentheses. Hand over the mouth, like at the lawyer's office in April. Then down again.

He knew, she said. I hadn't told him. I had a card picked out. The short laugh. I remember that fence. I said never again, and I didn't get in one for ten years. Today was going to be the first time. He never once did what you did on the hood of my car. She held the notebook on her knees with both hands. He'd have taken her today. He'd have left the water and gone. It probably would've been fine. He'd have called your mom from the car.

Probably fine. We chart that at work. It's not a vital sign. She gave the notebook back. September, seven AM. I read the bottom of your sheet. She got out, then leaned back in with one hand on the roof. Bring the scale.
At 9:40 that night, in Aurora, the phone buzzed twice in a row.
A text from Lourdes Reyes. Claire told me. You told the baby no. Good. I am proud of you mija. I am still not getting in that airplane.
A text from Abby Strand. Right call. Next is pattern work. Crosswinds, go arounds, slips, and you landing it every time. Walt says he's coming to watch. Ignore him. You won't be able to.

She read both of them twice, standing at the counter in her socks. Then she got the legal pad out of her bag, turned to a clean page, and wrote SEPTEMBER at the top of it, and under that, in her own small handwriting, the weights she'd measured that afternoon, every one of them, so she wouldn't have to ask anybody again.
